summary: Defines extensions to the Internet MIB for managing DECnet Phase IV, reflecting operational experience with RFC 1289.

plainLanguage.summary: DECnet is a Digital Equipment company network. This memo adds gauges so a manager can check on it with Internet tools.

subtitle: A set of SNMP managed objects that lets IP-based management stations monitor and control DECnet Phase IV systems, especially routers.

tldr.problem: Networks often ran DECnet Phase IV alongside TCP/IP, and managers wanted to manage both from one IP-based management station instead of separate tools.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the DECNET-PHIV-MIB, a tree of managed objects under mib-2 18 written in the Internet SMI and carried by SNMP, built from the DIGITAL Network Management Functional Specification Version 4.0.0.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 1289 with fixes from operational experience, including new adjacency objects, obsoleted old ones, and several groups moved from mandatory to optional.

facts.label: Node address
facts.value: 2 octets, area in the top 6 bits

sections.title: Managing DECnet with Internet Tools
sections.content:
RFC 1559 defines a set of DECnet Phase IV extensions to the Internet MIB. It reflects operational experience with RFC 1289, and was produced by the DECnet Phase IV MIB working group of the IETF.

The motivation is practical. With SNMP, the Internet MIB and the SMI widely implemented, network managers wanted to use that environment for integrated management of multi-protocol networks. DECnet Phase IV was one widely used protocol that often coexisted with IP. This memo lets IP-based management stations manage DECnet Phase IV systems, especially router products, through the standard Internet SMI, MIB and SNMP.

Support for other DECnet-based protocols such as RBMS (Remote Bridge Management Software), or for other Digital Equipment Corporation hardware platforms, is not included.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks spoke two languages. This memo lets one manager use one set of tools to look after both, instead of learning two sets.

sections.title: The Management Framework It Plugs Into
sections.content:
The memo relies on the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, which has three parts: the SMI (RFC 1155, with RFC 1212 for a more concise description form), MIB-II (RFC 1213) as the core set of managed objects, and SNMP (RFC 1157) as the access protocol.

Managed objects live in a virtual information store, the Management Information Base. They are defined with a subset of ASN.1. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and an object type plus an instance identifies one specific instantiation of the object. A human-readable text descriptor is used as a convenient name.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a rulebook for how to write down and ask about things on a network. This memo just adds new pages about DECnet to that rulebook.

sections.title: Selected Objects and Groups
sections.content:
The objects were created from the DIGITAL Network Architecture Network Management Functional Specification Version 4.0.0, dated July 1983. The memo tried to keep each object's original syntax. For example, Executor State was a NICE (Network Information and Control Exchange) coded one-byte field, and became an enumerated integer in the Internet MIB. Descriptors were taken from the original specification and adjusted to match the style of the standard Internet MIB. The term EXECUTOR refers only to the DECnet software on the system, not to other protocols running there.

The objects are ordered into 14 groups: System, Network Management, Session, End, Routing, Circuit, DDCMP, DDCMP Multipoint Control, Ethernet, Counters, Adjacency, Line, Non Broadcast Line and Area. The whole tree sits at phiv ::= { mib-2 18 }.

Each group states whether implementing it is mandatory or optional. Several are optional, and the text says a system implements those groups only if it implements all objects in them. Examples of the stated rules: the Routing Layer Group is mandatory for systems that implement level 1 routing, the Ethernet Group for systems that support ethernet links, and the Area Parameters Group for systems that implement level 2 routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo sorts everything you could ask a DECnet machine into fourteen labelled drawers, like routing, circuits and areas. Some drawers every machine must have, and some are optional.

sections.title: Textual Conventions and Object Types
sections.content:
Three new data types are introduced to make the objects easier to understand. No change to the SMI or SNMP is needed to support them.

  • PhivAddr is a 2-octet string holding a DECnet Phase IV node address. The area number is in the most significant 6 bits of the first octet. The next 2 bits of that octet are the first two bits of the host address, and the second octet holds the rest.
  • PhivCounter is an integer used for DECnet counters. Counters latch at their maximum value until the system restarts or the user or management software resets them to zero.
  • InterfaceIndex is an integer with the range of ifIndex, 1 to 2147483647.

Objects use the usual access modes such as read-only and read-write. For example, phivSystemState is a read-write enumeration with the values on (1), off (2), shut (3) and restricted (4). The RFC notes these are incremented by one compared to the standard DECnet values, to comply with RFC 1155.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo invents a few simple kinds of boxes to hold answers: one for addresses, one for counters that stop at the top instead of starting over, and one for numbering network interfaces.

sections.title: Examples of What Can Be Managed
sections.content:
The Definitions section is most of the document. A few samples show the style. In the System Group, phivSystemState sets whether the node allows logical links: ON allows them, OFF allows no new links and terminates existing ones, SHUT allows no new links but lets existing ones finish before going to OFF, and RESTRICTED allows no new incoming links from other nodes. phivExecIdent is a text description of the node of up to 32 characters.

In the Session Group, phivSessionSystemName is a node name of 0 to 6 characters, where 0 means no name, and phivSessionInTimer is the maximum time in seconds between a connect arriving and the process accepting or rejecting it. The Routing, Circuit, DDCMP, Ethernet, Adjacency, Line and Area groups hold similar parameters and tables for those parts of a DECnet system.

The Area Group has a table with one row per known area, indexed by phivAreaNum (0 to 64). Each row records the area state (reachable or unreachable), cost, hops, next node and circuit index. I skimmed the large circuit, DDCMP and line tables and describe them here only by their purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Each drawer holds questions you can ask, such as 'is this machine on?' or 'how far away is that area?'. Some answers you can only read, and some you can change.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1289
sections.content:
Section 6 lists what changed from RFC 1289:

  • Ranges were added to all PhivCounter types to remove ambiguity, and all indexes are made clear to start with 1.
  • Spelling, typographic and consistency fixes, including removing subranging within table entry sequences, plus updated compliance text and a fix to the phivControlMaxBuffs description and range mismatch.
  • phivRouteType and phivRouteSystemAddr became obsolete. They are replaced by the read-write objects phivRouteRoutingType and phivRouteSystemAddress.
  • A new adjacency table was added as adjacency 2, indexed by phivAdjNodeCircuitIndex and phivAdjAddr. It is identical to the old one except that phivAdjExecListenTimer was not carried over. The old table and all its objects are obsolete.
  • Two counter objects, phivCountersCountDataBlocksRecd and phivCountersCountDataBlocksSent, became obsolete because they overlapped the retained DataBlks versions.
  • The Session, End, DDCMP, DDCMP Multipoint Circuit Control, Counters and Non Broadcast Line groups moved from mandatory to optional.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the list of fixes since the last version: some messy old entries were retired and replaced with cleaner ones, and some groups became optional.
